newsitem.title: JAPAN: Impact of Mississippi closure limited- grain trade.
newsitem.headline: Impact of Mississippi closure limited- grain trade.

text.p: East Asian buyers said on Wednesday they expect only limited impact on the grains and oilseeds markets from the closure of the Mississippi River after a barge accident, unless the blockage continues for a few weeks.

"Theoretically, the accident is bearish news for Chicago grain futures market and bullish for the U.S. cash market. But everything depends on how many days the river will be closed," a corn trader at a major Tokyo commodity house said.

A group of 25 barges being towed on the Missisippi on Monday evening broke loose after colliding with a bridge in north Baton Rouge, causing the U.S. Coast Guard to close the affected section of the river. Traffic was still halted late on Tuesday.
Some Japanese soybean traders said they may be forced to look at Brazilian soybeans if the Mississippi, a key transport artery for U.S. agricultural exports, remains closed for several weeks.
"If we actually face supply concerns, we're going to have to cover more Brazilian soybeans and will pay higher premiums," one soybean trader in Tokyo said.

A trader with South Korea's National Livestock Cooperatives Federation said the barge accident could boost grain prices on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) later on Wednesday by raising fears over nearby U.S. grain and oilseed shipments.
But an official with an edible oil producer in Seoul said the news could push soybean prices lower in the mid-term by cutting U.S. soybean exports.
Traders in Taiwan expected the barge accident to have little impact on grain and oilseed futures prices unless the river remains closed for more than a week.
"A few days of shipment delay will not have much impact on futures prices," a trader in Taipei said.
The traders said they were more concerned with major fundamental changes like the weather and crop planting acreages.
"We need to watch out for news like wet weather in parts of the U.S. Midwest and forecasted floods," one said.
Their comments were echoed in Singapore by a trader dealing with the Southeast Asian grain and oilseeds market.
"Buyers here are mostly looking at Chinese corn and are taking Argentina or Brazil for their soybean and soymeal requirements. U.S. origins are not in the picture at the moment," he said.

CBOT May soybeans were a touch higher at $8.31-1/2 a bushel at 0600 GMT on the exhange's Project A after-hours trading system after rallying during the Chicago session. May soymeal was up 30 cents at $269.60 a ton.
CBOT May corn was unchanged on Project A at $3.01 a bushel after closing lower in Chicago on talk of more Chinese exports and on expectations of higher deliveries on the March position.

Yen-based corn futures on the Tokyo Grain Exchange were weaker in the morning session on Wednesday, probably because most domestic investors were not aware of the Mississippi accident, local traders said. All the Tokyo contracts were down, with the benchmark position 40 yen lower at 16,030 yen a tonne.
The Japanese government currently holds nearly 800,000 tonnes of corn and 400,000 tonnes of barley in feed grain stockpiles, which would be released in case of supply shortages.

"We're aware of the barge accident on the Mississippi River, and are monitoring developments. But there's no urgency to prepare for the emergency release of our grain stocks at the moment," an official at the Agriculture Ministry said.
